surfaces.part: stair treads (repeating snow steps, 8-row period, e.g. first full tread)
flanking rock cliff wall (left and right edges)

answer.evidence: Every step repeats the same pattern. Rows 8-11 are 4 rows of pale snow tread (L~236), and row 12 is a white front-edge line (L=255). Rows 13-15 are three darker riser or eave-shadow rows (#71819a, #566479, #3c4658). This gives about 5 rows of top surface above 3 rows of vertical riser per step, which is the tread-edge-shadow-riser structure of a 3/4 view. The same cycle repeats at rows 16-23, 24-31 and so on to row 63, so the staircase reads as climbing north. The top step at rows 0-7 follows the same pattern. The flanking dark rock strips at the left and right form the cliff cut and are a vertical south face. Rows 64-79 are flat ground.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a snow stair with white and pale-blue treads, blue-grey risers and dark rails. It has about 4 lightness steps per material, against about 5-6 in the references. The outline is tinted blue-grey rather than neutral black, which matches the 0% near-neutral dark edge share. The measured 8 visible tones per tile is at or above the paving reference (7) and grass (3), so the numbers alone do not make it shallow. By eye, though, it falls short of the references. The treads repeat as clean stripes with almost no grain, speckle or per-step variation. The tan landing at the bottom is a large flat block of one colour with no dots, and the exact flat-fill measure is 16% against 0% for both references. The references show per-stone shading and grass tufts throughout, and this piece is flatter and more sticker-like. When in doubt, fail.
